This legislation funded the movement of the federal government from Philadelphia to the new capital city of Washington, D.C.
To help lawmakers perform their legislative duties, the 1800 law provided $5,000 to purchase necessary reference books.
The original order contained 740 books and 3 maps purchased directly from legal and literary dealers in London.
Disaster struck during the War of 1812 when invading British troops burned the U.S. Capitol building in August 1814.
This devastating fire destroyed the entire founding library collection, which had grown to nearly 3,000 volumes.
To rebuild the national collection, former President Thomas Jefferson sold his personal library of 6,487 books to Congress in 1815 for $23,950.
Jefferson's vast personal collection contained books on science, philosophy, and literature, effectively laying the foundation for modern library operations.

article1.title: Article 1: Guglielmo Marconi b. 1874 (invented wireless telegraph) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Guglielmo Marconi revolutionized world communication by proving that messages could travel across vast distances without physical wires.
In December 1901, he achieved a historic breakthrough by transmitting the first transatlantic wireless signal over 2,100 miles from England to Newfoundland, Canada.
Marconi's wireless telegraph system quickly became an essential safety tool for ships traveling across the ocean.
When the RMS Titanic struck an iceberg in April 1912, operators used Marconi's equipment to send distress signals that saved over 700 passengers.
His remarkable engineering achievements earned him international recognition and prestigious awards.
In 1909, Marconi shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work in developing practical radio communications.
Today, Marconi is remembered as the father of radio and modern long-distance communication.
His early experiments laid the technological groundwork for modern radio broadcasting, cellular phones, Wi-Fi networks, and satellite technology.

article2.title: Article 2: Guglielmo Marconi b. 1874 (invented wireless telegraph) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Guglielmo Giovanni Maria Marconi was born in Bologna, Italy, on April 25, 1874.
Growing up in a wealthy family, he showed a passion for physics and electrical engineering at an early age.
In 1894, twenty-year-old Marconi began conducting secret radio experiments in the attic of his family's estate.
Using simple homemade equipment, he successfully rang a telegraph bell across the room without using any connecting wires.
By 1895, Marconi improved his transmitters and receivers to send wireless signals over a distance of 1.5 miles.
Finding little interest from the Italian government, he moved to England in 1896 to seek funding and patent protection for his invention.
In July 1897, Marconi registered his first patent and founded the Wireless Telegraph and Signal Company in London.
His early commercial success established the foundation for global radio communication networks in the twentieth century.

article1.title: Article 1: Hubble Space Telescope deployed 1990 - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: On April 25, 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope was released into orbit by Space Shuttle Discovery, changing astronomy forever.
By orbiting 340 miles above Earth's atmosphere, it bypassed atmospheric blur to capture remarkably clear images of the universe.
Over its decades in space, Hubble has taken more than 1.5 million observations and helped scientists determine the age of the universe to be about 13.8 billion years.
It also discovered that the expansion of the universe is accelerating due to a mysterious force called dark energy.
Beyond science, Hubble captivated the public with stunning color photographs of distant galaxies, glowing nebulas, and star-forming regions.
Famous images like the 'Pillars of Creation,' captured in 1995, brought the wonders of deep space into classrooms and homes worldwide.
Astronauts visited the telescope five times between 1993 and 2009 using space shuttles to upgrade its instruments and repair components.
Even as newer observatories launch, Hubble remains an invaluable tool for global research and continues to inspire future generations of space explorers.

article2.title: Article 2: Hubble Space Telescope deployed 1990 - Origins & History
paragraphs: The idea for a space telescope was first proposed by astrophysicist Lyman Spitzer in 1946, decades before the technology existed to build one.
He realized that a telescope placed above Earth's atmosphere could see fainter objects without distortion from air currents and light pollution.
In the 1970s, NASA joined forces with the European Space Agency to design and construct the massive observatory.
Originally named the Large Space Telescope, it was renamed in 1983 in honor of Edwin Hubble, the astronomer who proved that other galaxies exist outside our Milky Way.
Although planned for launch in 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster delayed the mission for several years while safety systems were re-evaluated.
Finally, on April 24, 1990, Space Shuttle Discovery launched from Kennedy Space Center, deploying the telescope into orbit the following day on April 25, 1990.
Shortly after deployment, scientists discovered a tiny flaw in the main mirror, which was ground incorrectly by 1/50th the thickness of a human hair.
In December 1993, astronauts aboard Space Shuttle Endeavour successfully installed corrective optics, fixing its vision and ensuring its place in history.

article1.title: Article 1: Jackie Joyner-Kersee famous Olympian (awarded 2007) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Jacqueline Joyner-Kersee is widely recognized as one of the greatest female athletes of all time.
Across four consecutive Olympic Games between 1984 and 1996, she captured six medals, including three gold, two silver, and one bronze.
At the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul, South Korea, she set the world record in the heptathlon with an amazing score of 7,291 points.
Decades later, her 1988 heptathlon performance still stands as the highest world-record score in track and field history.
In 2007, she was awarded the NCAA Theodore Roosevelt Award, which is the highest honor given by the college sports organization to a former student-athlete.
This prestigious 2007 recognition highlighted her extraordinary athletic accomplishments as well as her lifelong dedication to leadership.
Beyond the track, she created the Jackie Joyner-Kersee Foundation to help thousands of young students succeed in academics and sports.
Her incredible achievements paved the way for future generations of female athletes around the world.

article2.title: Article 2: Jackie Joyner-Kersee famous Olympian (awarded 2007) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Jackie Joyner-Kersee was born in East St. Louis, Illinois, on March 3, 1962.
She was named after First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy, and her family encouraged her to work hard and aim high from a very young age.
As a young teenager growing up in Illinois, she began competing at the local Mary Brown Community Center.
By high school, she was an all-state star athlete in track, basketball, and volleyball, jumping over 20 feet in the long jump.
Her outstanding high school accomplishments earned her a athletic scholarship to compete for UCLA.
At UCLA from 1980 to 1985, she starred on the women's basketball team while simultaneously building a world-class career in track and field.
She qualified for her first United States Olympic team in 1984, winning a silver medal in the heptathlon at age 22.
Her early days at UCLA and in East St. Louis laid the foundation for her historic journey to becoming a world champion.

article1.title: Article 1: John James Audubon b. 1785 (ornithologist & artist) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: John James Audubon created one of the most remarkable natural history works in human history, titled The Birds of America.
Published between 1827 and 1838, this monumental collection contained 435 life-sized, hand-colored prints depicting 497 different bird species.
The original copperplate engravings were printed on massive paper sheets measuring 39.5 inches tall by 29.5 inches wide so that every bird could be drawn at its actual size.
Audubon completely transformed how scientists and artists depicted wildlife.
Unlike earlier illustrators who drew birds using stiff, stuffed taxidermy models, Audubon used flexible wire frames to set freshly gathered specimens into active, natural poses.
His dynamic dynamic visual style brought scientific illustration to life and influenced generations of artists and naturalists across the globe.
Audubon's work helped launch the modern conservation movement in the United States.
In 1905, environmental pioneers named the newly established National Audubon Society in his honor to protect wild bird populations and preserve natural habitats.
Today, this organization operates more than 40 national nature centers and manages millions of acres of bird sanctuaries across North America.
Beyond his artwork, Audubon made lasting contributions to early American ornithology.
He personally identified and described 25 new bird species and 12 new subspecies during his extensive travels.
His detailed field observations provided valuable scientific data that researchers still reference over 170 years after his death in 1851.

article2.title: Article 2: John James Audubon b. 1785 (ornithologist & artist) - Origins & History
paragraphs: John James Audubon was born Jean-Jacques Audubon on April 26, 1785, in Les Cayes, Saint-Domingue, which is modern-day Haiti.
He was the son of Lieutenant Jean Audubon, a French naval officer, and Jeanne Rabine, a French woman who died just months after his birth.
In 1791, as slave rebellions broke out in Saint-Domingue, young Audubon was moved to Nantes, France, where his stepmother raised him.
Growing up in France during the turbulent years of the French Revolution, Audubon developed a passionate interest in the natural world.
He spent much of his childhood exploring the French countryside, collecting bird nests, eggs, and small animals.
Without any formal academic training in natural science, he taught himself how to sketch and paint the local wildlife.
In 1803, at the age of 18, Audubon immigrated to the United States to escape conscription into Napoleon Bonaparte's army.
He settled at his family's farm at Mill Grove, near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where he continued his passion for studying native birds.

It was at Mill Grove in 1804 that he conducted the first known bird-banding experiment in North America, tying silver threads to the legs of eastern phoebes to prove they returned to the same nesting sites each spring.
By 1820, after several failed business ventures in Kentucky, Audubon made the bold decision to pursue his dream full-time.
He set off down the Mississippi River with his gun, artist supplies, and a young assistant, pledging to paint every bird species on the continent.
His tireless journey over thousands of miles transformed a self-taught immigrant into the world's premier wildlife illustrator.

article1.title: Article 1: Frederick Law Olmsted b. 1822 (designed Central Park) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Frederick Law Olmsted transformed American cities by creating the profession of landscape architecture in the nineteenth century.
His most famous achievement was New York City's Central Park, an 843-acre green space designed alongside architect Calvert Vaux in 1858.
Olmsted believed that accessible public parks were essential for the physical and mental health of all urban citizens.
Throughout his career, he designed over 500 public spaces, including Prospect Park in Brooklyn and Boston's 1,100-acre Emerald Necklace park system.
Beyond city parks, Olmsted played a vital role in the early American environmental conservation movement.
In 1865, he wrote a landmark report urging the protection of Yosemite Valley, and in 1885, he helped establish the Niagara Falls Reservation state park.
Today, Olmsted is widely celebrated as the father of American landscape architecture.
Millions of people every year continue to enjoy his historic green spaces, which remain vibrant sanctuaries in major American cities.

article2.title: Article 2: Frederick Law Olmsted b. 1822 (designed Central Park) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Frederick Law Olmsted was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on April 26, 1822.
As a young boy, he developed a deep appreciation for the outdoors during long family rides through the New England countryside.
Before becoming a designer, Olmsted tried several different careers during his twenties and thirties.
He worked as a merchant sailor in 1843, operated a farm on Staten Island in 1848, and traveled through the American South as a journalist for The New York Times in the 1850s.
A major turning point occurred in 1857 when Olmsted was appointed superintendent of the land set aside for Central Park.
In 1858, he partnered with English architect Calvert Vaux to submit the winning design, known as the Greensward Plan, chosen out of 33 entries.
During the American Civil War from 1861 to 1863, Olmsted served as the executive secretary of the United States Sanitary Commission.
After the war, he dedicated the rest of his life to designing public park systems and college campuses until his retirement in 1895.

article1.title: Article 1: Samuel Morse b. 1791 (invented Morse Code) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Before Samuel Morse introduced the single-wire electric telegraph, long-distance messages took days or weeks to travel by horseback or ship.
By revolutionizing communication in the 1840s, Morse made it possible to send information across hundreds of miles in just a few seconds.
In 1844, the first official telegraph line connected Washington, D.C., to Baltimore, Maryland, over a distance of 44 miles.
Businesses and newspapers quickly adopted Morse code, allowing news outlets like the Associated Press, founded in 1846, to share global headlines almost instantly.
Railroad companies used Morse's invention to coordinate train schedules and prevent dangerous train collisions starting in the 1850s.
During the American Civil War from 1861 to 1865, President Abraham Lincoln sent over 1,000 telegrams to communicate directly with his military generals on the battlefield.
By 1866, the first successful transatlantic telegraph cable spanned over 2,000 miles across the Atlantic Ocean, connecting Europe and North America.
Today, Samuel Morse is remembered as a pioneer whose invention laid the foundation for modern telecommunications, including the internet.

article2.title: Article 2: Samuel Morse b. 1791 (invented Morse Code) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Samuel Finley Breese Morse was born on April 27, 1791, in Charlestown, Massachusetts.
He attended Yale College, graduating in 1810 at age 19, where he studied religious philosophy, mathematics, and electricity.
After college, Morse traveled to England to study art and became a successful portrait painter in the United States.
In 1825, while painting in Washington, D.C., he received news by slow horse-drawn mail that his wife was ill, but she had already died and been buried by the time he returned home to Connecticut.
Grief-stricken by the delay in communication, Morse became determined to find a faster way for people to transmit messages across great distances.
In 1832, while returning from Europe on a ship, Morse learned about electromagnetism, sparking his idea for an electric telegraph.
Working with assistant Alfred Vail, Morse developed a system of dots and dashes in 1837 to represent numbers and letters of the alphabet.
On May 24, 1844, Morse famously sent the first official telegraph message, "What hath God wrought," proving his invention was a success before his death in 1872.

article1.title: Article 1: Ulysses S. Grant b. 1822 (18th U.S. President) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: General Ulysses S. Grant led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War, ultimately accepting General Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865.
His decisive military leadership preserved the United States as one nation and helped secure freedom for over 4 million formerly enslaved African Americans.
As the 18th President of the United States from 1869 to 1877, Grant actively worked to protect the civil rights of newly freed Black citizens.
He signed the Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871 to combat violent white supremacist groups like the Ku Klux Klan and enforce the 15th Amendment.
During his two terms in office, Grant also established Yellowstone as the world's first national park on March 1, 1872.
In addition, he resolved peaceful diplomatic disputes with Great Britain through the 1871 Treaty of Washington, avoiding another costly international war.
In 1885, while suffering from severe throat cancer, Grant completed his personal memoirs just days before his death to secure financial stability for his family.
Published by Mark Twain, his memoirs sold over 300,000 copies and are still considered one of the greatest military autobiographies ever written.

article2.title: Article 2: Ulysses S. Grant b. 1822 (18th U.S. President) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Ulysses S. Grant was born Hiram Ulysses Grant in Point Pleasant, Ohio, on April 27, 1822.
Growing up in Georgetown, Ohio, his father operated a tannery, but young Grant disliked that work and preferred caring for horses on the family farm.
In 1839, at age 17, Grant was appointed to the United States Military Academy at West Point.
A clerical error by Congressman Thomas L. Hamer accidentally registered him as 'Ulysses S. Grant,' a name he decided to adopt for the rest of his life.
After graduating in 1843, Grant served as a quartermaster in the Mexican-American War from 1846 to 1848, learning valuable tactical skills under General Zachary Taylor.
He resigned from the army in 1854 and struggled with several civilian jobs in Missouri and Illinois over the next seven years.
When the Civil War broke out in 1861, Grant rejoined the military as a colonel in the 21st Illinois Infantry Regiment.
His brilliant military strategy, starting with a major victory at Fort Donelson in February 1862, quickly propelled him to Commander of all Union armies by 1864.

article1.title: Article 1: James Monroe b. 1758 (5th U.S. President) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: James Monroe served as the 5th President of the United States from 1817 to 1825, leaving a lasting mark on American foreign policy.
His presidency was defined by major diplomatic achievements that shaped how the world viewed the growing nation.
In December 1823, he delivered a speech that introduced the famous Monroe Doctrine to the U.S. Congress.
This policy warned powerful European nations not to interfere in or colonize any country in the Western Hemisphere.
During his two terms in office, the nation experienced a period of unity known as the Era of Good Feelings.
He also signed the historic Missouri Compromise of 1820, which attempted to balance free and slave states in the growing country.
Monroe expanded the physical borders of the nation by negotiating the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, which acquired Florida from Spain.
By the time he left office in 1825, Monroe had firmly established America as a confident and expanding force in world politics.

article2.title: Article 2: James Monroe b. 1758 (5th U.S. President) - Origins & History
paragraphs: James Monroe was born on April 28, 1758, in Westmoreland County, Virginia, into a modest family of landowners.
Growing up on a farm, he learned practical skills alongside basic academic studies before pursuing higher education.
In 1774, at age 16, he enrolled at the College of William and Mary to study classical subjects and law.
However, when the American Revolutionary War broke out, he left school in 1776 to join the Continental Army.
As a young officer, Monroe saw action at the Battle of Trenton on December 26, 1776.
He was severely wounded by a musket ball in his shoulder during the battle, but he recovered and was promoted for bravery.
After his military service, Monroe studied law under Thomas Jefferson, who became a valuable lifelong mentor.
This legal and political training helped him serve as a U.S. Senator, Governor of Virginia, and diplomat before he was elected president in 1816.

article1.title: Article 1: Andre Agassi b. 1970 (tennis player) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Andre Agassi left an unforgettable mark on the sport of tennis through his incredible achievements on the court.
During his professional career, he won eight Grand Slam singles titles and earned the world number one ranking.
One of his greatest career highlights occurred at the 1996 Summer Olympic Games in Atlanta, Georgia.
Agassi won the gold medal in men's singles, making him one of the very few male players to achieve a Career Golden Slam by winning all four major titles and Olympic gold.
Beyond his tournament victories, Agassi transformed tennis culture during the late 1980s and 1990s.
His bold fashion choices, including colorful shirts and denim shorts, inspired millions of young fans to start playing tennis.
After retiring from professional tennis in 2006, Agassi dedicated his life to education and charitable causes.
Through the Andre Agassi Foundation for Education, established in 1994, he has raised over 180 million dollars to build charter schools and support underprivileged youth.

article2.title: Article 2: Andre Agassi b. 1970 (tennis player) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Andre Kirk Agassi was born on April 29, 1970, in Las Vegas, Nevada.
Growing up in a busy household, he began hitting tennis balls at age two under the strict instruction of his father, Emmanuel Agassi.
Recognizing his exceptional natural talent, his family sent him to train at the famous Nick Bollettieri Tennis Academy in Florida when he was thirteen years old.
His fast hand speed and powerful return of serve quickly set him apart from other junior players in the country.
In 1986, at just sixteen years old, Agassi officially turned professional and entered the world tennis circuit.
By 1988, at age eighteen, he had already won six professional tour titles and accumulated over two million dollars in prize money.
Agassi captured his very first major tournament championship in 1992 by winning the Wimbledon singles title in London.
This dramatic victory proved his ability to compete at the highest level and launched a historic career that spanned twenty years.

article1.title: Article 1: Duke Ellington b. 1899 (jazz musician) - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: Edward Kennedy 'Duke' Ellington fundamentally changed the landscape of music as an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra.
From 1923 until his death in 1974, he continuously led his ensemble for over 50 years, establishing standard techniques for big band arrangements.
Ellington composed more than 1,000 original pieces, creating legendary works such as 'It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)'.
His remarkable artistic output earned him 13 Grammy Awards and inspired generations of musicians across the globe.
He helped elevate jazz from popular dance entertainment to a recognized form of fine art, often referring to his style as 'American Music'.
In 1969, Ellington received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the United States, for his cultural contributions.
His international tours during the 1950s and 1960s introduced American jazz culture to audiences in Europe, Asia, and Latin America.
In 1999, on the 100th anniversary of his birth, he was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize Special Citation for his lifetime of musical genius.

article2.title: Article 2: Duke Ellington b. 1899 (jazz musician) - Origins & History
paragraphs: Duke Ellington was born in Washington, D.C., on April 29, 1899, to two musical parents.
He began studying classical piano at age 7, though he was initially more interested in playing baseball than practicing music.
As a young teenager, his classy manners and stylish clothing earned him the nickname 'Duke' from his friends.
At age 15 in 1914, while working at a local ice cream shop, he composed his very first song, 'Soda Fountain Rag'.
Driven by his growing passion for ragtime and jazz, Ellington moved to New York City during the Harlem Renaissance in the early 1920s.
He organized his first major band in 1923 and secured a famous long-term residency performing at Harlem's Cotton Club in 1927.
Weekly live radio broadcasts from Harlem's Cotton Club carried Ellington's unique band sound to millions of homes nationwide.
By the 1930s, these performances launched him into national stardom, laying the foundation for his lifelong career as a legendary jazz pioneer.

article1.title: Article 1: National Arbor Day - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: National Arbor Day has grown from a local event into a major national celebration observed on the last Friday of April each year.
This civic holiday inspires communities across the country to come together to plant trees and care for the environment.
The environmental impact of this tradition is staggering, with millions of trees planted every single year.
Since its establishment in 1972, the Arbor Day Foundation alone has helped plant and distribute more than 500 million trees worldwide.
In thousands of schools across all 50 U.S. states, students participate in annual tree-planting ceremonies and environmental lessons.
These efforts help create healthier urban forests, clean our air, and provide vital natural habitats for local wildlife.
Today, the spirit of Arbor Day has expanded far beyond American borders to over 40 countries around the world.
More than 150 years after its creation, this holiday continues to demonstrate how individual actions can make a lasting global difference.

article2.title: Article 2: National Arbor Day - Origins & History
paragraphs: The story of Arbor Day began in 1854 when pioneer J. Sterling Morton moved from Michigan to the treeless plains of the Nebraska Territory.
As a journalist and nature lover, Morton quickly realized that trees were essential for windbreaks, soil protection, fuel, and building materials.
On January 4, 1872, Morton proposed an official tree-planting holiday to the Nebraska State Board of Agriculture.
The board approved his idea, setting the very first Arbor Day celebration for April 10, 1872, and offering prizes to counties that planted the most trees.
The initial event was an overwhelming success, resulting in an estimated 1 million trees planted in Nebraska in just a single day.
Impressed by this incredible community effort, Nebraska declared Arbor Day an official state holiday two years later in 1874.
Over the next century, tree-planting traditions spread across the nation as environmental awareness continued to grow.
In 1970, President Richard Nixon officially proclaimed National Arbor Day as a national observance, establishing its permanent date on the last Friday of April.

article1.title: Article 1: Vietnam War ended 1975 - Impact & Legacy
paragraphs: On April 30, 1975, the long and costly Vietnam War officially came to an end when North Vietnamese forces captured the southern capital city of Saigon.

Just hours before military hostilities concluded, Operation Frequent Wind used helicopters to evacuate over 1,000 American personnel and nearly 7,000 Vietnamese refugees to U.S. Navy ships waiting offshore.
The war left severe long-term scars, resulting in the deaths of more than 58,000 American service members and an estimated 2 million Vietnamese civilians.
Following the fall of Saigon, hundreds of thousands of South Vietnamese citizens, often referred to as boat people, fled the country in small boats to seek safety abroad.
After the conflict ended in 1975, North and South Vietnam were formally merged into a single nation named the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in 1976.
To mark the conclusion of the war, the new government officially renamed the city of Saigon to Ho Chi Minh City in honor of their political leader.
The painful experience in Vietnam fundamentally altered American foreign policy, creating decades of caution regarding overseas military conflicts.
Today, the events of 1975 serve as a major historic lesson in global diplomacy, human displacement, and the devastating impacts of modern warfare.

article2.title: Article 2: Vietnam War ended 1975 - Origins & History
paragraphs: The Vietnam War began in November 1955 after Vietnam won independence from French colonial rule and was divided into North and South Vietnam along the 17th parallel.
Communist leader Ho Chi Minh governed North Vietnam, while a non-communist government backed by the United States led South Vietnam during the global Cold War.
Direct American military involvement escalated rapidly after the United States Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in August 1964.
By 1969, the conflict reached its peak intensity with more than 500,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Southeast Asia.
Growing opposition to the conflict triggered massive anti-war demonstrations across American cities and college campuses throughout the late 1960s and early 1970s.
In January 1973, the United States signed the Paris Peace Accords, which resulted in the complete withdrawal of American combat forces by March 1973.
Despite the peace agreement, fighting between North and South Vietnamese armies continued without direct American military ground assistance.
In early 1975, North Vietnamese forces launched a final military offensive across the country, culminating in the surrender of South Vietnam on April 30, 1975.
